lead: This unit explains how sinusoidal AC voltages are generated, measured and drawn as phasors. It shows how R, L and C behave in series AC circuits and how active, reactive and apparent power are separated. It ends with balanced three-phase star and delta systems, line and phase quantities, and three-phase power.
about: The unit starts with 2.1, where a coil rotating in a magnetic field gives v = V<sub>m</sub> sin ωt, and average and RMS values turn a waveform into useful numbers. 2.2 compares those numbers through form factor and peak factor for sine and rectified waves. 2.3 replaces sine waves by rotating phasors, so addition and subtraction become complex-number work. 2.4 uses phasors to find impedance, current and phase angle in R-L, R-C and R-L-C series circuits. 2.5 separates active, reactive and apparent power and defines power factor. 2.6 introduces three-phase star and delta connections, and 2.7 derives line and phase relations and the √3 power formulas for balanced loads.

chapters.idea: A rotating coil in a magnetic field produces a sine wave whose peak, average and RMS values let us compare it with DC.
chapters.depth: Cover generation from a coil rotating at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field: e = E<sub>m</sub> sin ωt, where e is instantaneous voltage in V, E<sub>m</sub> is peak voltage in V, ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s and t is time in s. Use E<sub>m</sub> = N B A ω, where N is number of turns, B is flux density in T and A is coil area in m². Define instantaneous value, peak value, cycle, period T, frequency f = 1/T and angular frequency. Define average value over a half cycle for a sine wave: V<sub>avg</sub> = 2V<sub>m</sub>/π. Define RMS value: V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√2, and explain that it gives the same heating as a DC value. Some syllabi call RMS the effective value. Use RMS for AC meters and power unless stated.

figure.aria: Plot of a 325 V peak sine wave with horizontal lines at plus and minus 230 V RMS.

chapters.example: A sinusoidal voltage is v = 325 sin(314t) V. Find peak, RMS, half-cycle average and frequency. Solution: V<sub>m</sub> = 325 V; V<sub>rms</sub> = 325/√2 = 229.8 V ≈ 230 V; V<sub>avg</sub> = 2×325/π = 206.9 V; ω = 314 rad/s, so f = 314/(2π) = 50 Hz.
chapters.trap: The full-cycle average of a pure sine is zero; the quoted average value is over a half cycle or over a rectified wave. Use RMS, not peak, in power formulas unless stated.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: resistance, voltage, current; basic trigonometry and radians.
chapters.leave: Faraday's law, magnetic flux density and magnetic circuits are developed in Unit 3; safety, fuses and earthing are in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Form factor and peak factor are two ratios that describe waveform shape using its RMS, average and peak values.
chapters.depth: Define form factor = V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>avg</sub>, where V<sub>rms</sub> is RMS value and V<sub>avg</sub> is average of the rectified waveform. Define peak factor = V<sub>m</sub>/V<sub>rms</sub>, where V<sub>m</sub> is peak value. Compute for a sine wave: 1.11 and 1.414. Cover half-wave rectified sine (π/2 and 2), full-wave rectified sine (1.11 and 1.414), square and triangular waves. Some syllabi call peak factor the crest factor. State that average is taken over a half cycle for a pure sine, and over a full cycle for a rectified wave.

figure.title: Form factor and peak factor
figure.aria: Table comparing form factor and peak factor for sine, half-wave, full-wave, square and triangular waveforms.

chapters.example: A full-wave rectified sine has peak 100 V. Find average, RMS, form factor and peak factor. Solution: V<sub>avg</sub> = 2×100/π = 63.7 V; V<sub>rms</sub> = 100/√2 = 70.7 V; form factor = 70.7/63.7 = 1.11; peak factor = 100/70.7 = 1.41.
chapters.trap: Do not use the full-cycle average of a pure sine (it is zero) as the denominator; use the half-cycle average or the rectified average.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1: RMS and average values of a sine wave.
chapters.leave: Rectifier circuits belong to Unit 4; Fourier series of non-sinusoidal waves is outside this unit.

chapters.idea: A sinusoid of fixed frequency can be represented by a rotating arrow, or phasor, whose length is RMS or peak and whose angle is phase.
chapters.depth: Define phase, phase difference, lead and lag. Show the time domain v(t) = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt+θ) as a phasor V = V<sub>rms</sub>∠θ or a peak phasor; state the chosen convention. Cover Cartesian a+jb, polar r∠θ and exponential re<sup>jθ</sup>, where r is magnitude, θ is angle, a is real part and b is imaginary part; convert between forms. Add and subtract sinusoids of the same frequency by adding phasors. Some syllabi call this symbolic representation. Keep phasor magnitude convention consistent.

figure.title: Phasors add like vectors
figure.aria: Flow from two sine waves to phasors, rectangular addition, a sum phasor and back to a time expression.

chapters.example: v₁ = 10 sin(ωt+30°) V and v₂ = 20 sin(ωt−45°) V. Find v₁+v₂. Solution: use peak phasors V₁ = 10∠30° = 8.66+j5.00 V and V₂ = 20∠−45° = 14.14−j14.14 V. Sum = 22.80−j9.14 = 24.56∠−21.8°. So v = 24.56 sin(ωt−21.8°) V.
chapters.trap: Never add peak values directly when phases differ; convert to rectangular components. Keep degrees or radians consistent and add only same-frequency sinusoids.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1: sine wave, peak and RMS values; basic complex numbers.
chapters.leave: Impedance and circuit analysis are in Chapter 2.4; AC network theorems and resonance are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: In a series AC circuit, R, L and C combine as complex impedance, so current and voltage have both magnitude and phase.
chapters.depth: Define inductive reactance X<sub>L</sub> = ωL in Ω, capacitive reactance X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(ωC) in Ω, impedance Z = R+j(X<sub>L</sub>−X<sub>C</sub>) in Ω, and admittance Y = 1/Z in S. Analyze R-L, R-C and R-L-C series circuits: current I = V/Z, voltage across each element, phasor diagram, phase angle φ = tan⁻¹((X<sub>L</sub>−X<sub>C</sub>)/R), and leading or lagging. Cover simple parallel circuits through admittance. Some syllabi call this steady-state sinusoidal analysis or symbolic representation. Use RMS phasors.

figure.title: Series RLC solution steps
figure.aria: Flow from R, L and C values to reactance, net reactance, impedance, current and phase angle.

chapters.example: A series circuit has R = 30 Ω, L = 0.1 H, C = 50 μF and v = 230√2 sin(314t) V. Find Z, RMS current, phase angle and element voltages. Solution: X<sub>L</sub> = 314×0.1 = 31.4 Ω; X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(314×50×10<sup>−6</sup>) = 63.7 Ω; X = 31.4−63.7 = −32.3 Ω; Z = √(30²+32.3²) = 44.1 Ω; I = 230/44.1 = 5.22 A; φ = tan⁻¹(−32.3/30) = −47.1°, current leads voltage; V<sub>R</sub> = 156.5 V, V<sub>L</sub> = 163.8 V, V<sub>C</sub> = 332.3 V.
chapters.trap: Do not add R and reactances arithmetically; combine X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub> first, then use √(R²+X²). Use ω in rad/s, not f in Hz.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3: phasors; Unit 1: resistance, series circuits and Ohm's law.
chapters.leave: Resonance, AC Thevenin/Norton/maximum power, and transient response are outside this chapter; transients are in Unit 1 in some syllabi.

chapters.idea: AC power has three parts: active power that does work, reactive power that swings in L and C, and apparent power that sizes equipment.
chapters.depth: Define instantaneous power p(t) = v(t)i(t) in W. Define active power P = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>cos φ in W, reactive power Q = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>sin φ in var, and apparent power S = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub> in VA. Here φ is the angle by which current lags or leads voltage. Define power factor PF = cos φ = P/S. Explain lagging and leading by current relative to voltage. Introduce complex power S = P+jQ. Some syllabi call Q reactive volt-amperes. Keep RMS values.

figure.aria: Power triangle as a tree: apparent power splits into active power along cos φ and reactive power along sin φ.

chapters.example: A 230 V rms load draws 10 A rms at 0.8 power factor lagging. Find P, Q, S and the current phasor with voltage as reference. Solution: S = 230×10 = 2300 VA; P = 2300×0.8 = 1840 W; φ = cos⁻¹0.8 = 36.87°; Q = 2300×sin 36.87° = 1380 var; current lags by 36.87°, so I = 10∠−36.87° A if V = 230∠0° V.
chapters.trap: Standard power formulas use RMS values. Do not mix peak voltage with RMS current unless you apply the correct factor. Fix the sign convention before calling reactive power positive or negative.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4: impedance and phase angle; Chapter 2.1: RMS values.
chapters.leave: Two-wattmeter power measurement and tariffs are outside; see Unit 6 for energy meter, tariff and energy audit.

chapters.idea: Three-phase windings can be joined in star to give a neutral and two voltage levels, or in delta to form a closed three-wire loop.
chapters.depth: Explain three-phase generation: three voltages equal in magnitude and 120° apart, with phase sequence R-Y-B or A-B-C. Define phase voltage, phase current, line voltage and line current. Cover star (Y) connection: neutral point, line current equals phase current, and two voltage levels are available. Cover delta (Δ) connection: no neutral, line voltage equals phase voltage, and it is a closed three-wire loop. Some syllabi call star the Y connection and delta the mesh connection. State shared quantities here; derive the √3 relations in Chapter 2.7.

figure.aria: Left side shows a star connection with a neutral point; right side shows a closed delta loop with no neutral.

chapters.example: A balanced 400 V line-to-line, 50 Hz supply feeds a star-connected load with per-phase impedance 20∠30° Ω. Find phase voltage and phase current. Solution: V<sub>ph</sub> = 400/√3 = 230.9 V; I<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>/Z = 230.9/20 = 11.55 A; in star, line current = phase current = 11.55 A.
chapters.trap: Delta has no neutral, so do not connect a neutral to a delta load. Check whether the given voltage is line or phase before using it.
chapters.leave: The √3 line and phase relations and total power are in Chapter 2.7; unbalanced load analysis is beyond this unit.

chapters.idea: For balanced three-phase loads, line and phase quantities differ by √3, and total power is √3 V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>cos φ in both star and delta.
chapters.depth: Derive star relations: V<sub>L</sub> = √3 V<sub>ph</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>, where V<sub>L</sub> is line voltage, V<sub>ph</sub> is phase voltage, I<sub>L</sub> is line current and I<sub>ph</sub> is phase current. Derive delta relations: I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub> and V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>. Define φ as the angle between phase voltage and phase current. Derive total active power P = 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub>cos φ = √3V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>cos φ, reactive power Q = √3V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>sin φ and apparent power S = √3V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>. Some syllabi write V<sub>LL</sub> for line voltage. Use balanced loads only.

figure.title: Delta load power steps
figure.aria: Steps from a 400 V delta supply to phase current, line current, active power and apparent power.

chapters.example: A balanced delta load has phase impedance 15∠45° Ω and line voltage 400 V. Find phase current, line current, active power and apparent power. Solution: V<sub>ph</sub> = 400 V; I<sub>ph</sub> = 400/15 = 26.67 A; I<sub>L</sub> = √3×26.67 = 46.19 A; P = √3×400×46.19×cos 45° = 22.6 kW; S = √3×400×46.19 = 32.0 kVA.
chapters.trap: Do not put line current into P = 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub>cos φ; that formula uses phase values. In the √3 formula, φ is between phase voltage and phase current, not between any line quantities.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.6: star and delta connections; Chapter 2.5: active, reactive and apparent power.
chapters.leave: Two-wattmeter power measurement belongs to Unit 6; unbalanced load analysis and phase-sequence effects are not covered here.
